chunks.title: Episcleritis vs scleritis: the vessel test
chunks.tldr: Episcleritis = superficial vessels, mild, blanches with phenylephrine 10%. Scleritis = deep plexus, purple, severe boring pain, doesn't blanch.
points: 3 vessel layers: conjunctival (top, mobile), superficial episcleral (radial, straight), deep plexus (in the sclera).
Phenylephrine 2.5% blanches conjunctival vessels. 10% also blanches superficial episcleral vessels. Deep plexus doesn't blanch → scleritis.
Scleritis has a purple/violaceous tint best seen in daylight.
Episcleritis: common, benign, middle-aged women, often both eyes, lasts days to 3 weeks, recurs. Mostly idiopathic (sometimes RA, gout, Crohn, HZO, rosacea, CL).
Simple (75%): sectoral or diffuse redness, mild discomfort, VA normal. Peaks in 24 h.
Nodular: tender red nodule in the interpalpebral zone. Slit beam: scleral surface flat underneath (not scleritis).
Treat: nothing, cold tears, weak topical steroid 1–2 weeks, or oral NSAID.
chunks.hook: Episcleritis annoys. Scleritis destroys (and keeps you up at night).

cards.q: Which phenylephrine strength blanches superficial episcleral vessels?
How do you confirm a nodule is episcleral, not scleral?
cards.a: Slit beam shows a flat, non-elevated scleral surface beneath; nodule blanches/moves.

chunks.title: Anterior non-necrotizing scleritis
chunks.tldr: Diffuse or nodular. Deep pain that wakes them at night, radiates to the face/temple, painkillers barely help. Often linked to systemic disease.
points: Scleritis = whole-thickness scleral inflammation. Much rarer than episcleritis. May be the first sign of systemic disease.
Classification: anterior (non-necrotizing: diffuse, nodular; necrotizing: vaso-occlusive, granulomatous, surgically induced; scleromalacia perforans) and posterior.
Diffuse: women, ~40s. Red → pain days later, worst early morning. ± chemosis, uveitis, high IOP. Afterwards: grey-blue translucent sclera (rearranged fibres, not thinning).
Lasts ~6 years on average, recurs at the same spot.
Nodular: same age. Many have had HZO. Deep blue-red, immobile nodule; slit beam shows the sclera is raised. Doesn't blanch with phenylephrine 10%.
>10% of nodular cases progress to necrotizing.
chunks.hook: Scleritis pain = 3 am toothache in the eye.

cards.q: Bluish-grey area after scleritis resolves: thinning?
cards.a: No: increased translucency from fibre rearrangement (not true thinning).

chunks.title: Necrotizing scleritis & scleromalacia perforans
chunks.tldr: Necrotizing with inflammation = severe pain, white avascular patches, age ~60 → needs systemic immunosuppression (rituximab works well). Scleromalacia perforans = painless thinning in old women with RA.
points: Necrotizing: bilateral in 60%. Severe, constant pain to temple/jaw, ruins sleep.
Vaso-occlusive: RA. Patches of oedema with non-perfused (white) overlying tissue → necrosis.
Granulomatous: GPA, PAN. Starts at the limbus, everything raised and swollen within 24 h.
Surgically induced: within ~3 weeks of surgery (squint, trab with MMC, pterygium, buckle). Starts at the wound, stays in that sector.
Scleromalacia perforans (5%): elderly woman, long-standing RA. No pain, no redness. Yellow-white necrotic plaques → thinning → uvea shows through. Rarely perforates.
Complications of anterior scleritis: sclerosing keratitis, infiltrative keratitis, PUK, uveitis, glaucoma (commonest cause of vision loss), hypotony.
Investigate: ESR/CRP, FBC, RF, anti-CCP, ANA, ANCA, uric acid, syphilis, Lyme, Hep B, chest X-ray, anterior segment FA/ICG, B-scan.

chunks.title: Posterior scleritis
chunks.tldr: Younger (<40), often missed. Choroidal folds, exudative RD, disc oedema, pain on eye movement. B-scan 'T sign'.
points: Often under 40 and healthy. Over 55 → a third have systemic disease. Both eyes in 35%.
Pain variable (worse if myositis), photophobia not prominent.
Signs: horizontal choroidal folds, exudative RD (~25%), subretinal mass (can look like a tumour), uveal effusion, disc oedema (treat fast!), myositis (diplopia), mild proptosis.
Anterior scleritis only present in a minority.
B-scan: thick sclera, fluid in Tenon space → 'T sign' (optic nerve = stem, fluid = crossbar).
Differentials: choroidal tumour, VKH, CSR, orbital inflammation, TED, papilloedema.

cards.q: Characteristic B-scan sign of posterior scleritis?
cards.a: 'T sign': fluid in sub-Tenon space alongside the optic nerve.

chunks.title: Systemic links & treatment
chunks.tldr: RA = commonest association. GPA (cANCA), relapsing polychondritis, PAN (Hep B), Crohn. Non-necrotizing → oral NSAID. Necrotizing → systemic steroid + immunosuppressant.
points: Rheumatoid arthritis: commonest. Any scleritis type, more aggressive. Also dry eye, PUK.
GPA (Wegener): sinuses, lungs, kidneys. cANCA >90%. Necrotizing granulomatous scleritis, PUK, orbit, NLD.
Relapsing polychondritis: cartilage inflammation: floppy red ears, saddle nose, airway. Stubborn scleritis.
Polyarteritis nodosa: medium vessels, men 3:1, 1/3 Hep B. Aggressive necrotizing scleritis.
Crohn: episcleritis (tracks bowel activity), uveitis, marginal keratitis.
Treat: topical steroids = symptoms only. Oral NSAID for non-necrotizing only (watch GI bleeding; COX-2 in elderly).
Periocular steroid: NOT in necrotizing.
Oral pred 1–1.5 mg/kg or IV methylpred for necrotizing/NSAID failure.
GPA, PAN, necrotizing RA, polychondritis → immunomodulators straight away (cyclophosphamide, MTX, azathioprine, MMF, ciclosporin). Rituximab excellent for necrotizing.

chunks.title: Infectious scleritis & porphyria
chunks.tldr: Commonest infectious cause = herpes zoster. Also TB, leprosy, syphilis, Lyme, Pseudomonas, fungi. Think infection after surgery/trauma or if steroids make it worse.
points: Looks like immune scleritis at first. Can follow surgery, trauma, endophthalmitis, or spread from corneal infection.
Zoster: necrotizing, very stubborn, punched-out thinning.
TB: nodular or necrotizing. Leprosy: recurs even after cure. Syphilis: diffuse (secondary) or nodules (tertiary). Lyme: years after the bite.
Treat the bug ± steroids, debride if needed.
Porphyria (congenital erythropoietic, variegata, cutanea tarda): porphyrins in the sclera + sun → sharply demarcated interpalpebral thinning. Avoid sunlight, phlebotomy.

chunks.title: Scleral colours: blue, black, slate-grey
chunks.tldr: Blue = thin sclera: osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers–Danlos VI. Black = alkaptonuria (dark urine). Slate-grey patches = naevus of Ota → watch for glaucoma and uveal melanoma.
points: Osteogenesis imperfecta: type I collagen. Type I (AD): few fractures, deafness, blue sclera, megalocornea. Type IIA: multiple fractures, death in infancy.
Ehlers–Danlos VI (ocular-sclerotic): stretchy skin, loose joints, vascular rupture. Fragile sclera (ruptures with minor trauma), keratoconus, keratoglobus, ectopia lentis, myopia, RD.
Alkaptonuria (AR): homogentisic acid → ochronosis: dark sclera near the horizontal recti, urine turns black, arthritis.
Haemochromatosis: rusty-brown limbal discolouration, dry eye.
Congenital melanocytosis: slate-grey scleral/episcleral patches that don't move with the conjunctiva. Ocular only / skin only / both (naevus of Ota, V1/V2 skin).
Ota associations: iris hyperchromia, iris mammillations, fundus pigment, trabecular pigment → glaucoma ~10%, uveal melanoma (lifelong review).
Idiopathic sclerochoroidal calcification: elderly, yellow-white geographic fundus plaques along the arcades, very bright on ultrasound. Harmless.
Scleral hyaline plaque / senile scleromalacia: grey patches near horizontal recti insertions in the elderly. Harmless (not scleromalacia perforans).
